title: Four things that bring peace (III.23)
hook: do another's will, choose less, take the lowest place, want God's will
tomorrow: if God's gifts are good, why rest above them?

segments.voice: Yesterday the Imitation sang about love, and the first word on its list was swift. The line was nothing sweeter.

A group project, a family vacation, a playlist for the car: somebody has to give way. Can losing that argument actually bring you peace? The Imitation says yes, and then it does something strange. In chapter twenty-three of book three, Christ promises to teach the way of peace and true freedom. The disciple says, please, I love to hear it. And what comes next sounds less like peace than a list of ways to lose.
screen: `SOMEBODY HAS TO GIVE WAY.` → `THE WAY OF PEACE AND FREEDOM.` → `A LIST OF WAYS TO LOSE?`

segments.voice: Here's the list. Be eager to do another's will rather than your own. Choose always to have less rather than more. Look for the lowest place, and be willing to be beneath everyone. Wish always, and pray, that the will of God be fully done in you. Then the promise: whoever does this enters the borders of peace and rest. So the puzzle: how do losing your way, owning less and sitting in the back add up to peace? Look at what each one lets go of. The first loosens your grip on getting your way. The second, on having more. The third, on being seen. And the fourth turns the other three around: the point isn't losing, it's God's will, in Latin voluntas Dei. A clenched hand gets tired. Every grip you loosen is one less thing to defend. The disciple's reply holds the detail to tell a friend. This short word of yours, he says, holds much perfection: few words, full of meaning, rich in fruit. And he admits that whenever he feels upset and weighed down, he finds he has drifted from this teaching. That's the solution to the puzzle, in his own experience. The peace wasn't in winning. It was in not having to.
screen: `ANOTHER'S WILL, LESS, THE LOWEST PLACE.` · `AND GOD'S WILL, FULLY DONE.` · `EACH ONE LOOSENS A GRIP.` · `WHEN I'M UPSET, I'VE DRIFTED.` · then, large: `FOUR THINGS.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the four that will actually come up today: another's will, less, the lower place, or God's will. Picture the exact moment it will pinch, who's there and what you'll want to say. Then decide now what you'll do instead, and rest in that plan for the sit.
Four things that bring peace. Christ's short rule in the Imitation: another's will, less, the lower place, and God's will done in you.
screen: `FOUR THINGS THAT BRING PEACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: four things, few in words and full of meaning, as the disciple says. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1486 COUNTS.` → `THE IMITATION · 25 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: IF GOD'S GIFTS ARE GOOD, WHY REST ABOVE THEM?`

howItsDone: Catholics often read this chapter of the Imitation as a short rule for daily life, and some examine their day against it at night, asking where they held on and where they let go.

fork.setup: your roommate wants the window open, you want it shut, and it's the third night of this. which of the four does the chapter put first?

fork.reveal: the chapter's first thing is another's will before yours. it isn't about who's right; it's one less grip to hold.
